title: Felix and the Room
premise: Wren Kavanagh, a property surveyor, is hired to appraise the house where his grandmother died seven years ago — a house he has avoided ever since, telling himself the noises were pipes and settling wood. But every photograph of the house now contains an extra chair that wasn't there before, and when Wren touches the appraisal paperwork, the room pulls him inside: a version of the house that remembers everyone who ever signed for it. The last resident, a woman named Odile who has been 'resident' since 1961, must sign the papers to be released — but the signature requires singing the house's song through its final verse, and anyone who sings along becomes part of the furniture. Wren learns the verse from the house's previous victims, discovers his grandmother never escaped but bargained her memory away to spare him, and in the climax refuses to sing, instead offering the house the one thing it has never been given: an honest appraisal of what it lost. The house accepts truth over song; Odile signs freely, the extra chair empties, and Wren leaves carrying his grandmother's returned memories — including the price she paid to keep him out.
about_author: Mirabel Brightwater spent a decade as a historic-property assessor before turning to horror, drawing on the strange intimacy of appraising rooms where people died. She writes from a converted schoolhouse in coastal Maine, where she insists the chalkboards are original and nothing else is.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Sorting his grandmother's estate photos for probate, Wren notices every image of her house now includes a wooden chair that appears nowhere in his childhood memories. His partner jokes about Photoshop; Wren feels the old dread he's suppressed for seven years. Beat: denial cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: Appraisal Notice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The county assigns Wren the appraisal himself — conflict-of-interest waivers signed, no way to refuse without losing the contract. He drives out at dusk, tells himself it's just a house. The porch light turns on before he reaches the door. Beat: professional armor meeting personal terror.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, intercut with flashbacks. Inside, Wren catalogs damage while memories surface: the humming he heard as a child, grandma's rule never to sing indoors. He finds her old survey notes in the attic — her handwriting stops mid-sentence in 2018. Beat: the past insisting on relevance.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Answers
chapters.summary: Odile's POV (first shift). A woman in 1960s clothing appears in the parlor, courteous and exhausted, asking if he's 'the new signer.' Wren flees to his truck; the odometer reads zero miles driven. Beat: rationality formally surrendered.

chapters.title: Pulled
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Returning for his dropped clipboard, Wren touches the unsigned papers on the kitchen table and the room folds around him — same walls, wrong light, doors leading to decades. The chair from the photographs sits waiting at the table. Beat: threshold crossed, no return.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile explains the terms: the house releases whoever holds a completed deed, but the deed requires the song sung through its final verse — alone, correctly, without company joining in. Those who sang along became chairs, lamps, wallpaper. Beat: rules established, stakes named.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Lost
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren explores the folded house and finds rooms holding people half-absorbed: a mailman humming in a hallway, a child's voice inside a music box. He starts a surveyor's inventory — names, dates, conditions. Beat: grief converted into method.

chapters.title: Verse One Through Four
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile teaches Wren the first four verses, which she knows perfectly after sixty years. Each verse costs a memory to learn; Wren loses the smell of his grandmother's kitchen first. Beat: the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: What Grandma Signed
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the records room, Wren finds his grandmother's deed from 2018 — incomplete. She refused the final verse and instead traded all her memories of Wren to buy him immunity from being pulled. The blank space where his name should be in her mind explains her coldness in later years. Beat: devastating reframe of estrangement.

chapters.title: The Fifth Verse Problem
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. No resident has ever heard the fifth verse complete — the house hums it only during signings, and listeners always join in before it ends. Odile confesses she tried in 1974; her daughter sat down in the chair and stayed. Beat: guilt revealed, hope narrowed.

chapters.title: The Mailman's Ear
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren theorizes the verse can be learned without hearing it whole — assembled from fragments held by different absorbed residents. He negotiates with the mailman, trading memories for the three notes he caught in 1987. Beat: loyalty tested against exploitation.

chapters.title: Odile's Daughter
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Wren locates the girl inside the music box, still nine years old, still waiting for her mother to finish the song. Odile cannot bring herself to visit. Wren promises the girl they'll get her out. Beat: tenderness sharpening resolve into obligation.

chapters.title: Fragments
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Gathering pieces from residents across decades, Wren transcribes the fifth verse onto survey paper — but two bars are missing, and the house begins rearranging itself to slow him, hallways lengthening, doors forgetting their hinges. Beat: the house fights back.

chapters.title: The House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The house offers Wren a deal directly, through dreams: sign now, keep your memories, live long — someone else will finish the work someday. Wren wakes tempted, understanding why seven residents chose comfort. Beat: the seduction of deferral.

chapters.title: Two Bars Short
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. With the missing bars unfindable, Wren considers singing anyway and stopping before the end — Odile warns that a false ending traps the singer worse than absorption. Despair sets in; Wren nearly burns the transcription. Beat: darkest hour.

chapters.title: Grandma's Survey Notes
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Re-reading his grandmother's interrupted 2018 notes, Wren realizes the missing bars aren't hidden — they're unwritten. The fifth verse was always meant to be finished by the singer, not remembered. His grandmother stopped because she wouldn't invent an ending. Beat: revelation through craft.

chapters.title: Composing the Ending
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Wren and Odile argue over what the ending should say: vengeance, apology, release? Odile wants to apologize to the house; Wren insists the house deserves honesty, not flattery. They compose together, each bar costing them both memories. Beat: collaboration forged in sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Signing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At the kitchen table, pen ready, Wren sings verses one through four flawlessly. The house leans in, every absorbed resident going silent to listen. The chair beside him creaks closer. Beat: held breath before the leap.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, climactic. Wren sings the composed ending — an honest accounting of the house's losses: the family who abandoned it, the deaths it couldn't prevent, the loneliness it answered with capture. He does not invite anyone to join. The song completes; light floods the folded rooms. Beat: truth offered as payment.

chapters.title: Release
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Residents peel free — the mailman, the child, decades of the taken. Odile signs the deed with shaking hands and walks out into ordinary daylight for the first time since 1961, her daughter's hand in hers. The house exhales. Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: Closing Costs
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Outside, Wren files the appraisal: fair market value, condition honest, defects noted. The photographs lose the extra chair. He retains fragments of what he traded — enough to know something precious went, not enough to mourn precisely. Beat: bittersweet accounting.

chapters.title: The Song He Keeps
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, closing. Visiting his grandmother's grave, Wren hums the first verse softly — outdoors, where it's safe — and finds a returned memory surfacing: her voice teaching him the melody as a toddler, before everything. Some prices, he understands, come back as interest. Final line echoes the blurb: the noises have explanations; some of them are songs. Beat: quiet resolution with resonance.
